name: Baltic
intro: Baltic myth is the religious world of the Lithuanians, Latvians and Old Prussians, and it survives mostly in song. No Baltic pagan wrote down a connected pantheon. What remains comes from medieval chronicles and travellers' reports, from thousands of dainos and dainas recorded in the nineteenth century, and from folktales such as Eglė and the legends of amber. The sky god Dievas, the thunderer Perkūnas, the sun Saulė and the moon Mėnulis appear in short, vivid songs rather than in epic. This makes the tradition unusually open to reconstruction: the stories here join scattered verses, customs and later retellings, and they say where the joins show. Conversion, collecting and modern scholarship are part of the story too.

timeline.label: Baltic tribes and the amber coast
timeline.note: Baltic-speaking communities take shape between the Vistula and the Daugava. Amber from the coast travels south and west, but no written myth survives from this period.

timeline.label: Amber, Rome and the Aestii
timeline.note: Roman writers, including Tacitus, describe the Aestii gathering amber on the coast. Roman coins and imports reach the region, and offerings are left in bogs and waters.

timeline.label: The last pagan state
timeline.note: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania expands while the Teutonic Order crusades on its borders. Mindaugas is baptised in 1251, but the country returns to paganism, and Vilnius keeps its sacred fire and oaks.

timeline.label: Conversion
timeline.note: Jogaila converts Lithuania in 1387 and Samogitia follows in 1413. Christian teaching reshapes the old gods, but dainos, funeral customs and household rites carry much older material forward.

timeline.label: Chronicles and collectors
timeline.note: The sixteenth-century Sudovian Book and Jan Łasicki's 1582 account describe Prussian and Samogitian religion. In the nineteenth century Krišjānis Barons publishes Latvju dainas, while Lithuanian collectors and writers such as Maironis reshape the old songs.

timeline.label: Modern study
timeline.note: Archaeologists and folklorists such as Marija Gimbutas, Norbertas Vėlius, Endre Bojtár and Vykintas Vaitkevičius reconstruct Baltic religion and argue over how much can be recovered from song and soil.

sources.title: The Lithuanian dainos (folk songs)
sources.note: Short lyric songs collected from the nineteenth century onward in many regional variants. They preserve mythological motifs of the sun, moon, thunder, earth and the orphan, but not a connected narrative.

sources.title: The Latvian dainas
sources.note: Tens of thousands of four-line songs gathered by Krišjānis Barons and others and published in Latvju dainas (1894-1915). They are the richest source for Saule, Mēness, Pērkons and the dead.

sources.title: The Sudovian Book (Sūduvių knygelė)
sources.note: An anonymous sixteenth-century German account of Old Prussian and Sudovian religion, weddings and funerals. The original is lost and the text is known from later copies; its authorship and reliability are disputed.

sources.title: Maironis, 'Jūratė ir Kastytis'
sources.note: A ballad in the collection Pavasario balsai (1895) that fixed the modern form of the amber-sea legend, giving it the romance, the punishment and the tears.

sources.title: Marija Gimbutas, The Balts
sources.note: A wide-ranging survey of Baltic prehistory, culture and religion, first published in 1963. It remains useful but reflects the interpretive fashions of its time.

sources.title: Endre Bojtár, Foreword to the Past
sources.note: A cultural history of the Baltic peoples (1999) with careful discussion of the sources, the chronicles and the national myths built on them.

sources.title: Vykintas Vaitkevičius, Studies into the Balts' Sacred Places
sources.note: An archaeological study of sacred groves, stones, hills and springs, showing how cult sites can be identified and how cautiously they must be interpreted.
